COMPLETE EMPIRICAL RESEARCH PLAN  

================================================================  
1. IDENTIFICATION STRATEGY  
----------------------------------------------------------------  
Method: Difference-in-Differences (DID) combined with a shift-share (Bartik) design.

Logic  
• NAFTA generated plausibly exogenous, industry-specific tariff‐cut schedules that were written into the treaty years before they actually took effect.  
• Workers’ pre-NAFTA industrial composition is known from the 1990 Census.  
• Comparing wage changes between 1990 (pre) and 2000 (post) across industries and/or locations differentially exposed to these pre-determined tariff cuts yields the average causal effect of NAFTA-induced import competition on wage growth.  

Statistical model (worker i in industry j, area c, year t)  
log wage ijct = α + β (Post_t × TariffCut_j) + γ X_ijct + θ_j + λ_t + ε_ijct  

For geographic exposure we interact Post_t with LocalExposure_c, where
LocalExposure_c = Σ_j ( EmpShare_cj,1990 × TariffCut_j ).  
A triple-difference (DIDID) version can compare different education groups or tradable vs. non-tradable sectors.

Why appropriate  
• Clear policy shock with staggered, pre-announced intensity across industries.  
• Two sharply defined census snapshots straddling most of the liberalization period.  
• Rich micro data allow saturation of fixed effects and covariates to bolster parallel-trends credibility.

================================================================  
2. TREATMENT AND CONTROL  
----------------------------------------------------------------  
Treatment variable(s)  
A. Industry-level tariff cut  
 TariffCut_j ≡ Tariff_j,1990 – Tariff_j,2000  (continuous, % points)  

B. Geographic exposure  
 Exposure_c ≡ Σ_j ( EmpShare_cj,1990 × TariffCut_j )  

Control group  
Workers in industries (or areas) with zero or very small tariff reductions act as the implicit control. Because treatment is continuous, estimation compares more- versus less-exposed observations, conditioning on industry and year fixed effects.

Treatment timing  
Post_t = 1 for observations in the 2000 Census, 0 for 1990.

(If CPS or later Censuses are added, an event-study can trace effects annually.)

No RDD running variable is used; hence no cutoff.

================================================================  
3. KEY IDENTIFYING ASSUMPTIONS  
----------------------------------------------------------------  
A1. Parallel trends: In the absence of NAFTA, wage growth between 1990 and 2000 would have been similar across industries/areas with different scheduled tariff cuts.  
• Plausibility: Tariff schedule negotiated in 1992; little reason to correlate with unobserved 1990-2000 industry-specific wage shocks unrelated to trade.  

A2. Exogeneity of tariff schedule: The size and timing of tariff reductions were driven by international negotiations, not by contemporaneous U.S. labor-market conditions.  
• Plausibility: U.S. conceded faster liberalization in sectors where Mexico had latent comparative advantage, not where U.S. wage growth was forecast to be weak.  

A3. Stable unit treatment value (SUTVA): A worker’s wage is affected only by her own exposure, not directly by another industry’s tariff change except through the exposure measure we model.  
• Plausibility moderate; we will test for spillovers explicitly.  

A4. No systematic mobility that invalidates exposure measures: Workers do not sort endogenously into less-exposed industries/areas in anticipation of NAFTA in a way that is correlated with unobservables.  
• Addressed by instrumenting exposure with 1990 employment shares (“leave-one-out” when computing shares).

================================================================  
4. THREATS TO IDENTIFICATION & REMEDIES  
----------------------------------------------------------------  
T1. Concurrent China trade shock (1990-2000) biases results.  
 • Include industry-year controls for Chinese import penetration.  
 • Re-estimate after dropping top quartile of China-exposed industries.

T2. Differential pre-trends.  
 • Using 1980 Census or 1988–1992 CPS MORG, estimate placebo DID to test for pre-trend; include industry-specific linear trends if needed.

T3. Worker re-sorting across industries/areas.  
 • Baseline uses 1990 industry/area of work; run “stayer” subsample (workers whose industry does not change between 1990 and 2000).  
 • Use IV: instrument actual 2000 exposure with 1990 shares × tariff schedule.

================================================================  
5. R CODE OUTLINE  
----------------------------------------------------------------  
```r
# ----------- 0. Libraries ----------------
library(data.table)
library(fixest)      # fast high-dimensional fixed effects
library(readr)

# ----------- 1. Load Data ----------------
c90 <- fread("census_1990.csv")
c00 <- fread("census_2000.csv")
tariffs <- fread("tariff_mexico_8digit.csv")      # HS-8, 1990 & 2000
conv <- fread("hs8_to_census_industry_xwalk.csv") # concordance

# ----------- 2. Collapse tariff data to Census industries ----
tariffs <- merge(tariffs, conv, by = "hs8")
tariff_ind <- tariffs[, .(tariff90 = weighted.mean(tariff90, weight),
                          tariff00 = weighted.mean(tariff00, weight)),
                      by = census_industry]
tariff_ind[, TariffCut := tariff90 - tariff00]

# ----------- 3. Stack person-level data -----------
c90[, year := 1990]
c00[, year := 2000]
census <- rbindlist(list(c90, c00), use.names = TRUE, fill = TRUE)

# Log wages
census[, lwage := log(wage_income)]

# Merge tariff cuts
census <- merge(census, tariff_ind[, .(census_industry, TariffCut)],
                by = "census_industry", all.x = TRUE)

# Post indicator
census[, post := (year == 2000)]

# Controls
ctrls <- c("age", "I(age^2)", "female", "black", "hispanic", "married",
           "educ_hs", "educ_somecol", "educ_college")

# ----------- 4. Main DID regression -----------
form <- as.formula(
  paste0("lwage ~ post * TariffCut + ", paste(ctrls, collapse = "+"),
         " | census_industry + year"))
did1 <- feols(form, data = census, cluster = ~census_industry)
summary(did1)

# ----------- 5. Geographic exposure (shift-share) -----------
# 5a. Build 1990 employment shares by conspuma
share90 <- c90[, .N, by = .(conspuma, census_industry)]
share90[, total := sum(N), by = conspuma]
share90[, share := N / total]

# 5b. Exposure index
exposure <- merge(share90, tariff_ind[, .(census_industry, TariffCut)])
exposure <- exposure[, .(Exposure = sum(share * TariffCut)), by = conspuma]

census <- merge(census, exposure, by = "conspuma", all.x = TRUE)

# 5c. DID with shift-share
did2 <- feols(lwage ~ post * Exposure + post * TariffCut + 
                paste(ctrls, collapse = "+") | conspuma + year,
              data = census, cluster = ~conspuma)
summary(did2)

# ----------- 6. Robustness: drop top China-exposed industries ----
china <- fread("china_import_share.csv")
census <- merge(census, china, by = "census_industry", all.x = TRUE)
census_rb <- census[china_share < quantile(china_share, .75)]
did_rb <- feols(form, data = census_rb, cluster = ~census_industry)
summary(did_rb)
```

================================================================  
6. EXPECTED RESULTS  
----------------------------------------------------------------  
Economic theory (specific-factors and Heckscher–Ohlin) predicts that U.S. workers employed in sectors where Mexico has comparative advantage (e.g., low-skill, labor-intensive industries) face stronger wage pressure.  

Prior: A 1 percentage-point larger NAFTA-induced tariff cut will lower mean real wage growth of exposed U.S. workers by roughly 0.4–0.6 log points (≈0.4–0.6 %).  
Effects should be:  
• Largest (≈1 pp per ‑pt tariff) for ≤HS educated in directly exposed industries.  
• Moderately negative (≈0.2 pp per ‑pt) for local non-tradables via spillovers.  
• Near zero for college graduates and for workers in highly protected or capital-intensive industries.

================================================================  
7. VALIDITY CHECKLIST SELF-ASSESSMENT (for DID)  
----------------------------------------------------------------  
C1: No endogenous treatment timing  1  
C2: Parallel pre-trends confirmed   1 (will test w/ 1980-1990)  
C3: No simultaneous confounders    0 (China shock partially addressed)  
C4: Stable composition/no selective attrition 1 (1990 shares + stayer test)  
C5: Correct inference/clustering   1 (cluster at industry or area level)  

Total = 4 / 5 → reasonable but not bullet-proof.
